days.title: IAM Fundamentals: Users, Groups, Roles, and Policies

concepts.heading: The Four IAM Building Blocks
concepts.body: IAM revolves around four core objects: users (long-term identities for people or applications), groups (collections of users that share permissions), roles (temporary identities assumed by trusted principals rather than owned outright), and policies (JSON documents that define what actions are allowed or denied on which resources). Understanding how these fit together is the foundation for nearly every security question on the exam. A user or role has no permissions by default until a policy is attached, either directly or through a group. Grouping users by job function rather than attaching policies individually keeps permission management scalable as an organization grows.

concepts.heading: Policy Evaluation Logic
concepts.body: When AWS evaluates whether a request is allowed, it follows a strict order: an explicit Deny anywhere in any applicable policy always wins, overriding any explicit Allow. If there is no explicit Deny, an explicit Allow permits the action; if neither is present, the request is implicitly denied by default. This means a single Deny statement buried in one policy can block an action even if five other policies allow it. Exam questions frequently test this exact rule by describing conflicting policies and asking for the final outcome, so memorizing that explicit deny beats everything is essential.

concepts.heading: Identity-Based vs Resource-Based Policies
concepts.body: Identity-based policies are attached directly to a user, group, or role and describe what that identity can do. Resource-based policies, such as an S3 bucket policy or a KMS key policy, are attached to the resource itself and describe who can access it, including principals in other AWS accounts. Both policy types are evaluated together for any given request, and the results are combined using the same explicit-deny-wins logic. Resource-based policies are the mechanism that makes cross-account access possible without needing the accessing identity to assume a role in every case.

concepts.heading: Least Privilege and Access Analysis
concepts.body: The principle of least privilege means granting only the specific permissions required to perform a task, nothing more, which limits the blast radius if credentials are ever compromised. IAM Access Analyzer scans policies to identify resources shared with external entities and flags overly permissive grants, helping teams tighten policies without manually auditing every JSON document. Overly broad policies using wildcard actions or resources are a common exam distractor representing bad practice. Reviewing and right-sizing permissions periodically is considered a security best practice AWS expects candidates to recognize.

concepts.heading: Roles for EC2 Instead of Hardcoded Keys
concepts.body: When an application running on EC2 needs to call other AWS services such as S3 or DynamoDB, the recommended pattern is to attach an IAM role to the instance profile rather than embedding long-term access keys in code or configuration files. The EC2 instance metadata service automatically supplies short-lived, automatically rotated credentials to the application, removing the risk of leaked static keys. This pattern extends to Lambda functions, ECS tasks, and other compute services, all of which use execution roles for the same reason. Hardcoded credentials appearing anywhere in a scenario is almost always the wrong-answer signal on the exam.

examPoints: When a question describes one policy explicitly denying an action and another explicitly allowing it, the correct answer is always that the request is denied - explicit Deny overrides every Allow, with no exceptions.

If a scenario describes an EC2-hosted application needing programmatic access to another AWS service, look for the answer that attaches an IAM role to the instance rather than one that stores or hardcodes access keys.

quiz.q: A developer attaches two policies to the same IAM user: one allows s3:GetObject on a bucket, and the other explicitly denies s3:GetObject on the same bucket. When the user tries to read an object, what happens?
choices: The request is allowed because at least one policy grants access
The request is denied because explicit Deny overrides explicit Allow
AWS applies whichever policy was attached most recently
The request fails with a service error unrelated to permissions
quiz.explain: IAM always applies an explicit Deny over any explicit Allow, regardless of how many policies grant the permission. There's no policy ordering or 'most recent wins' concept in IAM evaluation, which rules out that option.

quiz.q: A company runs an application on EC2 that must upload files to an S3 bucket. Which approach follows AWS security best practices?
choices: Store an IAM user's access key and secret key in the application's configuration file
Attach an IAM role with the necessary S3 permissions to the EC2 instance profile
Use the AWS account's root user credentials for the application
Share one IAM user's credentials across all EC2 instances that need S3 access
quiz.explain: Attaching a role to the instance profile provides automatically rotated, temporary credentials with no keys to manage or leak. Hardcoding keys, using root credentials, or sharing one user's keys across instances all violate least-privilege and credential-hygiene best practices.

days.recap: IAM permissions are built from users, groups, roles, and policies, evaluated as explicit Deny > explicit Allow > implicit Deny, and EC2 workloads should use instance roles instead of embedded access keys.

days.title: Temporary Credentials and Cross-Account Access with STS and IAM Identity Center

concepts.heading: AWS STS and the AssumeRole API
concepts.body: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues temporary security credentials consisting of an access key, secret key, and session token, typically valid from 15 minutes up to several hours. The AssumeRole API call is the primary mechanism: a principal proves it is trusted, and STS returns short-lived credentials scoped to whatever permissions the assumed role's policy grants. Because these credentials expire automatically, they dramatically reduce the risk of long-term credential leakage compared to static IAM user access keys. Federation, cross-account access, and even AWS service-to-service calls all rely on STS under the hood.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Access with Trust Policies
concepts.body: To let a user in Account A access resources in Account B, Account B creates an IAM role with a trust policy naming Account A (or a specific principal in it) as allowed to assume it. The user in Account A then calls sts:AssumeRole against that role's ARN and receives temporary credentials scoped to Account B. This avoids ever creating duplicate IAM users or sharing long-term keys across account boundaries. An External ID can be added to the trust policy to prevent the 'confused deputy' problem when a third party assumes the role on your behalf.

concepts.heading: IAM Identity Center for Multi-Account SSO
concepts.body: IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides a single sign-on portal where employees log in once and see every AWS account and permission set they're entitled to, without needing an individual IAM user in each account. It integrates natively with AWS Organizations, assigning permission sets to users or groups across multiple accounts from one central place. This eliminates the operational burden of provisioning and deprovisioning IAM users account by account as staff join, move, or leave. It is the AWS-recommended replacement for manually managing IAM users at scale across an organization.

concepts.heading: Federation with External Identity Providers
concepts.body: Both STS and IAM Identity Center support federating with external identity providers using SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect (OIDC), allowing a corporate directory like Active Directory or an external IdP like Okta to be the source of truth for identity. Instead of creating AWS-native credentials for every employee, federated users authenticate against their existing corporate identity and are mapped to an IAM role that grants them AWS access. This is also the pattern used for web and mobile identity federation, and it keeps a single, centrally managed set of user credentials rather than duplicating accounts across systems.

examPoints: A scenario describing a large organization where employees need to log into multiple AWS accounts without individual IAM users in each one is a strong signal for IAM Identity Center.
A scenario describing temporary, time-limited access to resources in another AWS account points to STS AssumeRole combined with a cross-account IAM role and trust policy.

quiz.q: A partner company needs limited, temporary access to a specific S3 bucket in your AWS account. What is the most secure way to grant this?
choices: Share your account's root user credentials with the partner
Create a cross-account IAM role with a trust policy and have the partner use STS AssumeRole
Create an IAM user for the partner and email them the access keys
Make the S3 bucket public so the partner can access it directly
quiz.explain: A cross-account role combined with AssumeRole grants scoped, temporary credentials without sharing long-term secrets. Sharing root credentials, emailing access keys, or making the bucket public are all serious security anti-patterns.

quiz.q: Hundreds of employees across a company need to log into several AWS accounts using their existing corporate directory credentials, without provisioning a separate IAM user in every account. What service addresses this?
choices: Create an IAM user for each employee in every account
IAM Identity Center configured with centralized SSO
Share a single IAM user's credentials among all employees
Distribute long-term access keys to every employee
quiz.explain: IAM Identity Center centralizes sign-on across multiple accounts and integrates with external directories. Manually creating per-account IAM users or sharing credentials does not scale and violates least-privilege practices.

days.recap: STS AssumeRole issues short-lived credentials for cross-account access via a trust policy, while IAM Identity Center provides centralized single sign-on across many AWS accounts for an organization's workforce.

days.title: Multi-Account Governance with Organizations, SCPs, and Control Tower

concepts.heading: AWS Organizations and Account Grouping
concepts.body: AWS Organizations lets a company centrally manage multiple AWS accounts by grouping them into a hierarchy of organizational units (OUs), which mirror business units, environments, or teams. It also enables consolidated billing, combining usage across all member accounts onto a single invoice and often unlocking volume discounts. Centralizing accounts under Organizations is the prerequisite for applying organization-wide governance controls like SCPs and for using Control Tower. Most exam scenarios describing multiple AWS accounts under one company assume an Organizations structure is already, or should be, in place.

concepts.heading: Service Control Policies as Permission Ceilings
concepts.body: A Service Control Policy (SCP) is applied at the account or OU level and defines the maximum set of permissions available to every identity in that account, acting as a guardrail rather than a grant. Even if an IAM policy explicitly allows an action, an SCP that denies it will still block the request, because SCPs and IAM policies are combined with AND logic, not OR logic. SCPs never grant permissions on their own; actual permissions still come from IAM policies operating within whatever ceiling the SCP sets. A common exam trap describes a fully-permissive IAM policy and asks why access is still denied, expecting the answer that an SCP is blocking it.

concepts.heading: AWS Control Tower and Landing Zones
concepts.body: AWS Control Tower automates the setup of a secure, multi-account landing zone on top of Organizations, including a pre-built account structure, a Log Archive and Audit account, and a curated set of default guardrails built from SCPs and AWS Config rules. It significantly speeds up establishing a well-governed multi-account environment compared to configuring Organizations, SCPs, and logging manually from scratch. Control Tower also provides an Account Factory for automating the provisioning of new, compliant accounts as an organization grows. It is the AWS-recommended starting point for organizations building a new multi-account strategy rather than assembling one piece by piece.

concepts.heading: Guardrails vs Direct Permission Grants
concepts.body: It helps to keep a clear mental model: SCPs and Control Tower guardrails answer what is even possible in this account, while IAM policies answer what can this specific identity actually do within that boundary. A preventive guardrail (an SCP) stops an action outright, whereas a detective guardrail (an AWS Config rule) flags non-compliant resources after the fact without blocking them. Exam questions about blocking an entire region or service across dozens of accounts almost always expect an SCP-based answer rather than editing every account's IAM policies individually, since that would not scale and would be easy to circumvent.

examPoints: When a scenario needs to block a specific AWS region or service across many accounts at once, the SCP applied at the OU or account level is the scalable answer, not editing individual IAM policies.
If an IAM policy allows an action but the request is still denied, and the exam mentions an SCP, recognize that the SCP's ceiling overrides the IAM policy's grant.

quiz.q: A company wants to permanently prevent the use of a specific AWS Region across all fifty accounts in its organization. What is the most efficient way to enforce this?
choices: Edit the IAM policies in each of the fifty accounts individually
Apply a Service Control Policy at the organization or OU level that denies actions outside the approved Region
Change the root user password in every account
Add a deny statement to every S3 bucket policy
quiz.explain: An SCP applied at the OU or organization level enforces the restriction centrally across every account at once. Editing IAM policies account-by-account does not scale and could be bypassed by any new IAM policy.

quiz.q: An IAM policy grants a user permission to launch EC2 instances, but an SCP attached to that account denies ec2:RunInstances. What is the result when the user attempts to launch an instance?
choices: The request succeeds because the IAM Allow takes precedence
The request is denied because the SCP sets the maximum permission ceiling
AWS prompts an administrator to resolve the conflict manually
The request succeeds only in a designated safe region
quiz.explain: SCPs define the outer limit of what's possible in an account; an IAM Allow can never exceed that ceiling. There's no manual conflict-resolution step or region-based exception in this evaluation model.

days.recap: Organizations groups accounts under OUs with consolidated billing, SCPs act as non-granting permission ceilings that combine with IAM policies using AND logic, and Control Tower automates a governed landing zone with default guardrails.

days.title: Authenticating Application Users with Amazon Cognito

concepts.heading: Cognito User Pools for Authentication
concepts.body: Amazon Cognito User Pools act as a fully managed user directory for web and mobile applications, handling sign-up, sign-in, password resets, and multi-factor authentication for end users. After a successful login, the User Pool issues JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) that the application can use to verify the user's identity on subsequent requests. User Pools also support social identity providers like Google and Facebook, as well as enterprise SAML or OIDC providers, letting users sign in with credentials they already have. This service answers the question of who this end user is, independent of what AWS resources they might later access.

concepts.heading: Cognito Identity Pools for AWS Access
concepts.body: Cognito Identity Pools (also called Federated Identities) take an authenticated identity, whether from a User Pool, a social login, or even an unauthenticated guest, and exchange it for temporary AWS credentials via STS. Those credentials are scoped by IAM roles configured for authenticated and unauthenticated users, allowing the end user's mobile or web app to call AWS services like S3 or DynamoDB directly without a backend proxying every request. This division of labor is deliberate: User Pools authenticate, Identity Pools authorize access to AWS resources, and a single application typically needs both working together.

concepts.heading: Cognito vs IAM Identity Center: Internal vs External Users
concepts.body: A frequent point of confusion is which identity service applies to whom. IAM Identity Center is designed for a company's own workforce accessing AWS accounts and internal applications, while Cognito is designed for external, customer-facing end users of an application the company builds, such as a mobile app's registered users. Mixing these up is a common wrong-answer trap: a scenario describing customers signing up for an app calls for Cognito, while employees logging into the AWS console calls for IAM Identity Center. Recognizing this internal-versus-external distinction quickly narrows down the correct service on sight.

concepts.heading: Advanced Security Features and MFA
concepts.body: Cognito User Pools support advanced security features such as adaptive authentication, which scores each sign-in attempt for risk based on factors like device, location, and IP reputation, and can automatically require additional verification or block a login that looks suspicious. Multi-factor authentication can be enforced optionally or required for every user, using SMS codes or a time-based one-time password (TOTP) authenticator app. These features let a customer-facing application meet stronger authentication requirements without building fraud-detection or MFA infrastructure from scratch, which is often the deciding factor when a scenario specifically calls for protecting customer accounts against credential-stuffing or account-takeover attacks.

examPoints: A scenario where mobile or web app end customers sign up, log in, and then need to upload files directly to S3 points to Cognito User Pools for authentication combined with Identity Pools for temporary AWS credentials.
Distinguish internal employees (IAM Identity Center) from external application customers (Cognito) - this framing alone often eliminates two of the four answer choices.

quiz.q: A mobile app allows customers to register, log in, and then upload photos directly to an S3 bucket. What combination of services supports this most directly?
choices: Amazon Cognito User Pools for authentication plus Identity Pools for temporary AWS credentials
AWS Organizations with a shared IAM user
AWS STS used without any Cognito component
quiz.explain: Cognito User Pools authenticate the end customer, and Identity Pools exchange that identity for temporary AWS credentials scoped to S3 access. IAM Identity Center is meant for internal workforce access, not external app customers.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches the identity service to its intended audience?
choices: IAM Identity Center for internal employees, Cognito for external application customers
Cognito for internal employees, IAM Identity Center for external application customers
AWS Organizations for internal employees, STS for external customers
STS for internal employees, Organizations for external customers
quiz.explain: IAM Identity Center targets a company's own workforce accessing AWS accounts, while Cognito targets external end users of a company's applications. The other pairings reverse or misapply these roles.

days.recap: Cognito User Pools authenticate end users and issue JWTs, Identity Pools exchange that identity for temporary AWS credentials, and the whole service targets external application customers rather than internal staff, who use IAM Identity Center instead.

days.title: Threat Detection with Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Macie

concepts.heading: GuardDuty: Continuous Threat Detection
concepts.body: Amazon GuardDuty is a managed threat detection service that continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail management and data events, and DNS query logs to identify indicators of compromise such as communication with known malicious IP addresses, unusual API call patterns, or signs of a compromised credential being used to enumerate resources. It requires no agents to install and no infrastructure to manage; it simply needs to be enabled in a region. Findings are scored by severity and can trigger automated remediation through Amazon EventBridge, for example isolating a compromised instance or revoking a suspicious credential automatically.

concepts.heading: Macie: Discovering Sensitive Data in S3
concepts.body: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to scan objects stored in S3 to automatically discover and classify sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII), credentials, and financial data such as credit card numbers. Rather than manually auditing buckets, security teams can run Macie jobs against specific buckets or accounts and receive findings that flag exactly where sensitive data lives and whether it's exposed by an overly permissive bucket policy. This is particularly relevant for compliance requirements like GDPR or PCI-DSS, where knowing precisely where regulated data resides is a prerequisite for protecting it.

concepts.heading: Detection Target: Network/Account Activity vs Data Content
concepts.body: The clearest way to distinguish these two services is by what they actually inspect: GuardDuty looks at network traffic and API activity to catch behavioral threats, while Macie looks at the content of stored data to catch sensitive information exposure. A scenario about unusual login attempts or traffic to a known bad IP is a GuardDuty finding; a scenario about a bucket possibly containing unmasked social security numbers is a Macie finding. Both services surface results as structured findings and integrate with AWS Security Hub CSPM (the original Security Hub) for centralized visibility across a security operations workflow.

concepts.heading: Automated Remediation with EventBridge
concepts.body: Rather than requiring a security analyst to manually review every finding, both GuardDuty and Macie can publish findings to Amazon EventBridge, which routes them to a Lambda function, an SNS notification, or a Systems Manager Automation document that takes immediate remedial action. A common pattern is automatically attaching a restrictive network ACL or isolating security group to an EC2 instance the moment GuardDuty reports it as likely compromised, cutting the response time from hours of manual triage down to seconds. This event-driven remediation pattern is a recurring theme across AWS security services and is frequently the missing piece in scenarios asking how to respond to a threat automatically rather than just detect it.

examPoints: A requirement to automatically identify files in S3 containing personal or financial data points directly to Amazon Macie.
A requirement to detect unusual API activity, credential compromise, or communication with malicious IPs points directly to Amazon GuardDuty.

quiz.q: A company wants to automatically identify files uploaded to S3 that contain unredacted credit card numbers or national ID numbers. Which service should it use?
quiz.explain: Macie scans S3 object content to detect and classify sensitive data like PII and payment card numbers. GuardDuty, Shield, and WAF address network threats and traffic filtering, not data content.

quiz.q: A security team wants continuous monitoring for unusual API calls and communication with known malicious IP addresses across their AWS accounts. Which service fits this need?
quiz.explain: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs to detect exactly this kind of behavioral threat. Macie targets stored data content rather than network or account activity.

days.recap: GuardDuty continuously detects network and account-activity threats from logs, while Macie scans S3 data content to find sensitive information, and both can trigger automated response through EventBridge.

days.title: Application-Layer Protection: Shield, WAF, and Secrets Manager

concepts.heading: AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
concepts.body: AWS Shield Standard is automatically included at no extra cost for every AWS customer and defends against the most common network and transport layer (layer 3/4) DDoS attacks, such as SYN floods, by default on services like CloudFront and Route 53. Shield Advanced is a paid tier that adds protection against larger and more sophisticated DDoS attacks, near real-time visibility into attacks, 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT), and cost protection against scaling charges incurred during an attack. Organizations running business-critical internet-facing applications that are frequent DDoS targets typically justify the additional cost of Shield Advanced.

concepts.heading: AWS WAF for Layer 7 Filtering
concepts.body: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that inspects HTTP/HTTPS requests and blocks application-layer (layer 7) attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) based on configurable rules or AWS Managed Rule Groups covering common vulnerability patterns. It attaches to CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway, and AppSync, and can also implement rate-based rules to throttle abusive clients. Where Shield defends against volumetric network floods, WAF defends against malicious request content, making the two complementary layers of an internet-facing application's defense rather than substitutes for one another.

concepts.heading: Secrets Manager for Credential Storage and Rotation
concepts.body: AWS Secrets Manager stores sensitive values like database credentials, API keys, and OAuth tokens in encrypted form and, critically, supports built-in automatic rotation on a schedule for supported services like RDS, eliminating the need to hardcode or manually rotate passwords. Applications retrieve secrets at runtime via an API call rather than reading them from configuration files or source code, reducing the risk of accidental exposure through version control. Systems Manager Parameter Store offers a cheaper alternative for storing configuration values and secrets, but it does not include native automatic rotation, which is the key differentiator the exam expects candidates to know.

concepts.heading: Layering Shield, WAF, and Secrets Manager Together
concepts.body: A well-protected internet-facing application typically layers all three services rather than relying on just one: Shield absorbs large-scale network floods before they ever reach the application, WAF filters out malicious requests that do get through based on content, and Secrets Manager ensures that even if request-level defenses were somehow bypassed, the credentials the application relies on internally are never sitting exposed in code or configuration. Recognizing that these three services address different layers of the same overall threat model, rather than competing solutions to the same problem, helps rule out answer choices that substitute one for another when a scenario actually needs all three working together.

examPoints: A scenario describing SQL injection or cross-site scripting attacks against a web application points to AWS WAF rules, not Shield, which addresses network-layer floods instead.
A requirement to store database credentials outside application code and rotate them automatically on a schedule points to AWS Secrets Manager rather than Parameter Store.

quiz.q: A public-facing web application is being targeted by SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks. Which service should be configured to block these requests?
quiz.explain: WAF inspects and filters application-layer HTTP requests using rules that catch SQL injection and XSS patterns. Shield addresses network/transport-layer DDoS floods, not application-layer content attacks.

quiz.q: A team wants to remove hardcoded RDS database credentials from their application code and have those credentials rotate automatically on a schedule. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: Secrets Manager stores credentials securely and supports built-in automatic rotation for supported databases. Parameter Store could store the value but lacks native rotation, and the other services listed serve different purposes entirely.

days.recap: Shield Standard/Advanced defends against network-layer DDoS, WAF filters application-layer attacks like SQL injection and XSS, and Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates credentials so they never need to be hardcoded.

days.title: Data Protection: KMS Encryption, ACM Certificates, and AWS Backup

concepts.heading: AWS KMS and Encryption at Rest
concepts.body: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) creates and manages the cryptographic keys used to encrypt data at rest across most AWS services, including S3, EBS, RDS, and DynamoDB. Customers can use AWS-managed keys for convenience or create customer-managed keys (CMKs) with custom key policies for finer-grained control over who can use or administer them, and KMS integrates with CloudTrail so every key usage is logged for auditing. Because most storage services support encrypting with KMS as a checkbox-level integration, KMS is the default answer whenever a scenario requires encrypting data at rest with AWS-managed keys.

concepts.heading: Envelope Encryption
concepts.body: Rather than encrypting large volumes of data directly with a KMS master key, which would be slow and costly at scale, AWS uses envelope encryption: a unique data key is generated to encrypt the actual data, and that data key is itself encrypted by a KMS customer master key before being stored alongside the encrypted data. To decrypt, the application asks KMS to decrypt the small wrapped data key, then uses the resulting plaintext key locally to decrypt the actual data. This two-layer approach lets services encrypt large or many objects efficiently while still keeping the master key locked safely inside KMS.

concepts.heading: ACM for Encryption in Transit
concepts.body: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues and automatically renews free public SSL/TLS certificates that provision encryption in transit for services like CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway. Because ACM handles renewal automatically, it eliminates the operational risk of a certificate silently expiring and breaking HTTPS in production. The distinction the exam tests repeatedly is at-rest versus in-transit: KMS protects stored data, while ACM protects data moving between the client and AWS over the network, and a question describing either one is testing whether you know which layer it belongs to.

concepts.heading: AWS Backup for Centralized Backup Management
concepts.body: AWS Backup provides a single, policy-driven console for scheduling, managing, and monitoring backups across multiple AWS services, including EBS volumes, RDS and Aurora databases, DynamoDB tables, and EFS file systems, instead of configuring backup mechanisms separately for each service. Backup plans define schedule, retention, and lifecycle rules, such as transitioning older backups to cold storage, that apply consistently across resource types tagged for inclusion. This centralization is particularly valuable for organizations needing to demonstrate consistent backup compliance across a mixed fleet of resources for audits, rather than trusting that every team configured backups correctly on their own.

examPoints: Distinguish between encryption at rest (KMS manages the keys) and encryption in transit (ACM manages the TLS certificate) whenever a question separates stored data from data moving over the network.

A requirement to centrally manage and schedule backups across several different AWS services from one console points to AWS Backup rather than configuring each service's native backup feature separately.

quiz.q: A company wants data stored in S3 to be automatically encrypted with AWS managing the encryption keys. Which service handles this?
quiz.explain: KMS creates and manages the encryption keys used for encryption at rest across services like S3. Certificate Manager, Backup, and Shield address unrelated concerns: TLS certificates, backup scheduling, and DDoS protection.

quiz.q: A company needs a free SSL/TLS certificate for its CloudFront distribution and Application Load Balancer that renews automatically without manual intervention. Which service should it use?
quiz.explain: ACM issues and automatically renews public TLS certificates for use with CloudFront and ALB. KMS handles encryption keys for data at rest, not TLS certificates for data in transit.

days.recap: KMS manages encryption keys for data at rest using envelope encryption, ACM provides and auto-renews TLS certificates for encryption in transit, and AWS Backup centrally manages backup policies across multiple AWS services.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Secure Architectures

concepts.heading: Who Is Accessing: Identity Services Recap
concepts.body: Domain 1 opened with the identity layer: IAM users, groups, roles, and policies form the base permission model, evaluated as explicit Deny beating explicit Allow beating implicit Deny by default. STS AssumeRole and cross-account roles extend that model across account boundaries, IAM Identity Center centralizes workforce sign-on across many accounts, and Cognito authenticates external application end users before exchanging their identity for temporary AWS credentials. Recognizing whether a scenario describes an internal employee, an external customer, or a cross-account partner is usually the fastest way to pick the right identity service among these five.

concepts.heading: Governing at Scale: Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower
concepts.body: Once an organization has more than a handful of accounts, AWS Organizations groups them into OUs for centralized billing and management, Service Control Policies set non-granting permission ceilings enforced with AND logic against IAM policies, and Control Tower automates a compliant landing zone with default guardrails rather than assembling those pieces by hand. A scenario needing to block a region or service across dozens of accounts at once is an SCP problem, while a scenario needing a fast, best-practice multi-account setup from scratch is a Control Tower problem.

concepts.heading: Detect vs Protect: GuardDuty, Macie, Shield, WAF
concepts.body: The detection tools, GuardDuty for network and account activity and Macie for sensitive data discovered in S3, produce findings that describe what already happened or was found, while the protection tools, Shield for network-layer DDoS and WAF for application-layer attacks like SQL injection, actively block malicious traffic before it reaches the application. Grouping services this way, detect versus protect, resolves a large share of Domain 1 scenario questions quickly, since the question's verb usually reveals which category the correct answer belongs to.

concepts.heading: Protecting Data: KMS, ACM, Secrets Manager, Backup
concepts.body: The final Domain 1 theme is protecting data itself: KMS encrypts data at rest via envelope encryption, ACM provides TLS certificates for encryption in transit, Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates credentials so they're never hardcoded, and AWS Backup centrally manages backup policies across many services. These four rarely get confused with each other once you separate their exact jobs: key management, certificate management, credential management, and backup management are each a distinct concern even though all four sit under the protect-data umbrella of the domain.

examPoints: Before reading the answer choices, classify the scenario first: is it about who's accessing (identity), governing many accounts (Organizations/SCP), detecting versus blocking a threat, or protecting data - this narrows the field immediately.
Domain 1 is worth 30% of the exam, the largest single domain, so a shaky grasp on IAM policy evaluation or the SCP/IAM relationship disproportionately costs points.

quiz.q: Which of the following services is primarily a detection tool rather than an active protection or blocking mechanism?
quiz.explain: GuardDuty produces findings after analyzing logs; it detects threats rather than blocking traffic in real time. WAF and Shield actively filter or mitigate traffic, and ACM issues certificates, which is unrelated to threat detection.

quiz.q: Which service pairing correctly matches external application customers with internal company employees?
choices: Cognito for external customers, IAM Identity Center for internal employees
IAM Identity Center for external customers, Cognito for internal employees
STS for external customers, Organizations for internal employees
Organizations for external customers, STS for internal employees
quiz.explain: Cognito is purpose-built for external, customer-facing application users, while IAM Identity Center centralizes sign-on for a company's own workforce. The other pairings misassign these services' intended audiences.

days.recap: Domain 1 in one pass: identity (IAM/STS/Identity Center/Cognito) answers who's accessing, Organizations/SCP/Control Tower governs at scale, GuardDuty/Macie detect while Shield/WAF protect, and KMS/ACM/Secrets Manager/Backup protect data itself.

days.title: Building Loosely Coupled Architectures with SQS and API Gateway

concepts.heading: Why Loose Coupling Matters
concepts.body: Loose coupling means designing components so that a failure or slowdown in one part of the system doesn't cascade into every other part, typically by inserting an intermediary like a queue between a producer and a consumer instead of calling directly and synchronously. This is one of the core design principles behind resilient, scalable AWS architectures, because it lets each component fail, restart, or scale independently without taking the whole system down with it. Exam scenarios describing a downstream service becoming overwhelmed by a sudden traffic spike are almost always pointing toward introducing a buffering layer to decouple the two sides.

concepts.heading: SQS Standard vs FIFO Queues
concepts.body: Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queue that decouples producers from consumers asynchronously; a producer writes messages to the queue and consumers poll and process them independently, at their own pace. Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput and at-least-once delivery but do not guarantee message order or prevent occasional duplicates. FIFO queues guarantee strict ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group, but at lower throughput limits, making them the right choice when the sequence of operations matters, such as processing financial transactions in the order they occurred.

concepts.heading: Visibility Timeout and Message Processing
concepts.body: When a consumer retrieves a message from an SQS queue, that message becomes invisible to other consumers for a configurable visibility timeout, during which the consumer is expected to process and then explicitly delete the message. If the consumer crashes or takes longer than the visibility timeout to finish, the message reappears in the queue and may be processed a second time, which is why consumers should be designed to handle duplicate processing safely. Setting the visibility timeout too short causes redundant processing, while setting it too long delays retry of genuinely failed messages, so it should roughly match the expected processing time.

concepts.heading: API Gateway as a Managed API Front Door
concepts.body: Amazon API Gateway is a fully managed service for creating, publishing, and securing REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs that front backend targets like Lambda functions, EC2-hosted services, or even on-premises systems through a VPC Link. It handles cross-cutting concerns out of the box, including request throttling to protect backends from being overwhelmed, authorization via IAM, Cognito, or Lambda authorizers, and response caching to reduce backend load and latency. Combining API Gateway with Lambda is one of the most common serverless application patterns tested on the exam, since it removes almost all infrastructure management from the equation.

examPoints: A scenario describing a backend that becomes overloaded or crashes during traffic spikes is generally solved by placing an SQS queue between the producer and the backend to buffer and decouple the load.
A scenario emphasizing that message order must be strictly preserved, such as sequential payment processing, points specifically to an SQS FIFO queue rather than a standard queue.

quiz.q: An order-processing system experiences backend server crashes whenever traffic spikes suddenly. What architectural change would prevent this?
choices: Connect the frontend directly to the backend with synchronous calls
Insert an SQS queue between the frontend and backend to buffer requests asynchronously
Reject all incoming requests during high-traffic periods
Disable Auto Scaling on the backend fleet
quiz.explain: An SQS queue absorbs bursts and lets the backend process messages at a sustainable rate, which is the essence of loose coupling. Rejecting requests or disabling Auto Scaling would reduce availability rather than solve the underlying coupling problem.

quiz.q: A payment processing workflow requires that transactions be processed in the exact order they were submitted, with no duplicates. Which SQS queue type should be used?
choices: Simple HTTP polling of a database table
quiz.explain: FIFO queues guarantee both message ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group, which this scenario requires. Standard queues do not guarantee order and may deliver duplicates.

days.recap: Loose coupling isolates failures between components, SQS standard queues favor throughput while FIFO queues guarantee order and dedupe, visibility timeout controls how long a message stays hidden during processing, and API Gateway is the managed front door for REST/HTTP/WebSocket APIs.

days.title: Decoupling Compute: Lambda, ECS, EKS, and Fargate

concepts.heading: AWS Lambda for Event-Driven Serverless Compute
concepts.body: AWS Lambda runs code in response to events, such as an S3 upload, an API Gateway request, or a message arriving in an SQS queue, without requiring any servers to provision or patch. It automatically scales out to handle concurrent invocations, bills per millisecond of execution time, and is best suited to short-lived, stateless tasks, since a single invocation has a maximum execution duration of 15 minutes. Long-running or highly stateful workloads are a poor fit for Lambda and are a common wrong-answer signal when a scenario mentions something running continuously or for hours.

concepts.heading: Amazon ECS: AWS-Native Container Orchestration
concepts.body: Amazon ECS is AWS's own container orchestration service, where a task definition specifies the container image, CPU/memory, and networking configuration, and a service maintains a desired number of running task copies, replacing unhealthy ones automatically. ECS integrates tightly with other AWS services like ALB, CloudWatch, and IAM without needing to manage a separate control plane, making it a simpler on-ramp to containers than Kubernetes for teams already invested in the AWS ecosystem.

concepts.heading: Amazon EKS: Managed Kubernetes
concepts.body: Amazon EKS is a managed Kubernetes control plane, chosen when a team already runs workloads on Kubernetes and wants to preserve portability across clouds or on-premises environments, or needs specific Kubernetes ecosystem tooling that isn't available on ECS. EKS handles the operational burden of running and patching the Kubernetes control plane itself, but the mental model, API objects, and third-party tooling remain standard Kubernetes. A scenario mentioning an existing Kubernetes deployment being lifted to AWS is a strong signal for EKS over ECS.

concepts.heading: AWS Fargate: Serverless Compute for Containers
concepts.body: AWS Fargate is a launch type available for both ECS and EKS that removes the need to provision, patch, or scale the underlying EC2 instances that would otherwise host containers; you specify the CPU and memory a task needs, and AWS runs it on managed infrastructure behind the scenes. This trades some cost efficiency and low-level control for significantly less operational overhead, which makes it attractive for teams that want container flexibility without managing a fleet of EC2 hosts. A scenario emphasizing running containers without managing servers is describing Fargate specifically, regardless of whether the orchestrator is ECS or EKS.

examPoints: A scenario describing short, event-triggered tasks where no server management is wanted at all points to Lambda, while a scenario about running containers without managing EC2 hosts points to Fargate.
A scenario describing an existing Kubernetes-based deployment being migrated to AWS points to EKS specifically, not ECS, because it preserves the Kubernetes API and tooling.

quiz.q: An application needs to resize an image every time a new file is uploaded to S3, and the team wants zero server management for this short-lived task. What should they use?
choices: A permanently running Amazon EKS cluster
quiz.explain: Lambda is purpose-built for short, event-triggered tasks with no server management required. Running a permanent EKS cluster or EC2 instance for an occasional short task adds unnecessary operational overhead and cost.

quiz.q: A team wants to run containerized workloads on ECS but does not want to provision, patch, or manage the underlying EC2 instances. What should they choose?
choices: Install Docker directly on self-managed EC2 instances
AWS Fargate as the ECS launch type
quiz.explain: Fargate is the serverless launch type for ECS (and EKS) that removes EC2 instance management entirely. The other options either require managing servers directly or don't apply to container orchestration at all.

days.recap: Lambda handles short, event-driven serverless functions, ECS is AWS's native container orchestrator, EKS is managed Kubernetes for portability or existing Kubernetes workloads, and Fargate removes EC2 management from either orchestrator.

days.title: Workflow Orchestration and Layer 7 Load Balancing

concepts.heading: AWS Step Functions as a Visual State Machine
concepts.body: AWS Step Functions orchestrates a sequence of Lambda functions or other AWS service calls as a visual state machine, defined in the Amazon States Language, handling retries, error branching, and parallel execution declaratively instead of requiring custom orchestration code inside each function. Each step's success, failure, and timeout behavior is configured explicitly, and the entire execution history, including exactly which branch was taken and why, is retained for auditing and debugging. This makes it well suited to multi-step business processes where visibility into where exactly a step failed matters as much as the automation itself.

concepts.heading: Standard vs Express Workflows
concepts.body: Step Functions offers Standard workflows, which support executions up to a year long, exactly-once execution semantics, and a full execution history in the console, and Express workflows, which are optimized for high-volume, short-duration event processing at a lower cost with at-least-once semantics. Choosing between them depends on whether the workflow is a long-running, auditable business process (Standard) or a high-throughput streaming/data-processing pipeline where slight duplication is acceptable and cost efficiency matters more (Express).

concepts.heading: Application Load Balancer Routing
concepts.body: The Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7 and can route incoming HTTP/HTTPS requests based on path, such as routing /api to one target group and /images to another, host header, query string, or HTTP method, distinguishing it from Layer 4 load balancers that only see IP and port. ALB target groups can point to EC2 instances, containers via IP targets, or even Lambda functions directly, making it flexible across compute types within a single load balancer.

concepts.heading: Health Checks and Availability
concepts.body: ALB continuously performs configurable health checks against registered targets, checking a specified path and expected response code at a set interval, and automatically stops routing traffic to any target that fails enough consecutive checks, routing only to healthy targets thereafter. Combined with Auto Scaling replacing unhealthy instances, this health-check loop is a core mechanism behind maintaining availability without manual intervention when an individual instance degrades or crashes, and it's frequently referenced in exam scenarios about automatically removing failing servers from rotation.

examPoints: A scenario describing multiple service calls that must run in a specific order, with retry and failure handling and full visibility into each step, points to AWS Step Functions rather than a simple queue or manual scripting.

A scenario requiring routing to different backend services based on URL path or hostname points to Application Load Balancer, since Network Load Balancer operates below the application layer and cannot inspect that information.

quiz.q: An order fulfillment process runs payment, then inventory check, then shipping preparation, and needs automatic retries and full visibility into failures at each stage. What service fits best?
choices: A single SQS queue with no orchestration logic
AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow
Sequential script execution on a single EC2 instance
quiz.explain: Step Functions is designed exactly for multi-step orchestration with built-in retry logic, error handling, and execution visibility. An SQS queue alone or manual scripts lack this structured control and observability.

quiz.q: An application needs to route requests to different backend target groups depending on the URL path in the request. Which load balancer type should be used?
quiz.explain: ALB operates at Layer 7 and can inspect the URL path to route requests to different target groups. Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and cannot make routing decisions based on HTTP path.

days.recap: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows as a visual, retryable state machine, while ALB performs Layer 7 routing based on path or host header and continuously removes unhealthy targets from rotation via health checks.

days.title: High Availability Design: Availability Zones and Multi-AZ Architecture

concepts.heading: Availability Zones and Regions
concepts.body: An AWS Region is a geographic area containing multiple, physically separate Availability Zones (AZs), each consisting of one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, connected to other AZs in the same region via low-latency, high-throughput links. Because AZs are physically isolated, a failure in one, whether from a power outage, a natural event, or a hardware issue, is designed not to affect the others. This physical separation is the foundational building block that every high-availability pattern on AWS depends on.

concepts.heading: The Multi-AZ Pattern for High Availability
concepts.body: The most basic and important high-availability pattern on AWS is deploying redundant resources across at least two AZs, so that if one AZ becomes unavailable, the application keeps running from the surviving AZ. This applies broadly: an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs, an ALB distributing traffic across targets in multiple AZs, or a database maintaining a synchronously replicated standby in a second AZ. A scenario emphasizing that a single AZ outage should not take down the whole application is testing whether you know to spread resources across at least two AZs by default.

concepts.heading: High Availability vs Fault Tolerance
concepts.body: High availability tolerates a brief interruption followed by automatic recovery, such as a database failover that takes a minute to complete, while fault tolerance means the system continues operating with no perceptible downtime at all even during a component failure, which is a stricter and typically more expensive requirement to satisfy. The exam sometimes uses these terms precisely to distinguish between an architecture that recovers quickly (highly available) and one designed so failures are effectively invisible to end users (fault tolerant), so reading the requirement's exact wording matters.

concepts.heading: RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas
concepts.body: RDS Multi-AZ deployments maintain a synchronously replicated standby instance in a different AZ purely for availability; if the primary fails, RDS automatically fails over to the standby, but the standby cannot serve read traffic in the classic Multi-AZ configuration. Read Replicas, by contrast, are asynchronously replicated copies created specifically to offload read traffic from the primary and scale read performance, and they are not the automatic failover target unless explicitly promoted. Confusing these two, using a Read Replica when the requirement is availability, or expecting Multi-AZ to improve read throughput, is one of the most frequently tested mistakes in this domain.

examPoints: A requirement that the application must survive a single AZ failure without manual intervention almost always means the answer must involve deploying resources across at least two Availability Zones.

RDS Multi-AZ solves for availability via automatic failover, while Read Replicas solve for read-scaling; a scenario asking for both concepts in the same question is testing whether you can tell them apart.

quiz.q: A production database must automatically fail over to a standby with minimal downtime if its Availability Zone fails. Which configuration should be used?
choices: Use a larger instance in a single AZ
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ deployments maintain a synchronously replicated standby and perform automatic failover during an AZ outage. A Read Replica scales reads but is not the automatic failover target, and backups alone don't provide fast recovery.

quiz.q: What is the most fundamental design principle for ensuring an application survives the failure of a single Availability Zone?
choices: Concentrate all resources in a single AZ for simplicity
Distribute resources across at least two Availability Zones
Scale up a single instance to be as large as possible
Store backups only in a different Region
quiz.explain: Spreading resources across multiple AZs is the baseline pattern for surviving an AZ-level failure. Scaling a single instance up does nothing to protect against the AZ itself becoming unavailable.

days.recap: AZs are physically isolated data centers within a Region, high availability requires spreading resources across at least two AZs, and RDS Multi-AZ provides automatic failover for availability while Read Replicas separately scale read performance.

days.title: Route 53 Routing Policies and DNS-Based Resilience

concepts.heading: The Seven Route 53 Routing Policies
concepts.body: Route 53 supports seven routing policy types: Simple (a single static answer), Weighted (splits traffic by assigned percentages), Latency-based (routes to whichever region gives the client the lowest latency), Failover (routes to a primary resource, switching to a secondary if the primary is unhealthy), Geolocation (routes based on the user's geographic location), Geoproximity (routes based on geographic distance with an adjustable bias, requiring Route 53 Traffic Flow), and Multivalue Answer (returns multiple healthy IP addresses for basic client-side load balancing). Recognizing keywords like percentage of traffic, closest region, or automatic failover points directly to one of these seven policies.

concepts.heading: Failover Routing for Disaster Recovery
concepts.body: Failover routing pairs a primary and secondary resource record with Route 53 health checks: as long as the primary passes its health check, all traffic goes there, but the moment it fails, Route 53 automatically starts answering DNS queries with the secondary resource's address instead, all without any manual intervention. This is a foundational building block of DNS-based disaster recovery architectures, letting a standby environment in another region take over automatically when the primary region becomes unreachable, and it's a common component in questions about achieving cross-region resilience cheaply, since it doesn't require any active traffic-splitting infrastructure.

concepts.heading: Weighted Routing for Canary and Blue/Green Deployments
concepts.body: Weighted routing assigns a relative weight to each of multiple resource records serving the same domain name, letting a small percentage of traffic, say 10 percent, be directed to a new application version while the majority continues to the stable version, which is the classic canary deployment pattern. As confidence in the new version grows, the weight can be gradually shifted toward it until it receives 100 percent of traffic, completing a blue/green cutover entirely at the DNS layer, without needing any changes in the load balancer or application itself.

concepts.heading: Health Checks Powering Automated Routing
concepts.body: Route 53 health checks periodically probe an endpoint's IP address, hostname, or even a CloudWatch alarm state, marking the resource healthy or unhealthy based on the results, and several routing policies, particularly Failover and Multivalue Answer, rely directly on these health check results to decide which answers to return. Health checks can also trigger CloudWatch alarms and notifications independent of routing, giving operations teams visibility into endpoint status even outside of an active failover scenario.

examPoints: A scenario describing automatic traffic redirection to a disaster recovery region when the primary region fails points specifically to Failover routing, combined with Route 53 health checks.
A scenario describing sending only a small percentage of traffic to a new application version for testing points to Weighted routing, the DNS-layer equivalent of a canary release.

quiz.q: A company wants traffic automatically redirected to a disaster recovery region whenever its primary region becomes unhealthy. Which Route 53 routing policy should it configure?
quiz.explain: Failover routing works with Route 53 health checks to automatically redirect traffic to a secondary resource when the primary fails. Weighted and geolocation routing solve different problems: traffic percentage splits and location-based responses.

quiz.q: A team wants to gradually send a small, controlled percentage of production traffic to a new application version as part of a canary release. Which routing policy is appropriate?
quiz.explain: Weighted routing lets you assign a percentage of traffic to each version, which is exactly the mechanism a canary release needs. The other policies route based on latency, geography, or return multiple values rather than percentage splits.

days.recap: Route 53 offers seven routing policies; Failover automates DR traffic redirection using health checks, Weighted routing enables canary/blue-green traffic shifting, and health checks underpin the automated decisions several of these policies make.

days.title: Connection Resilience and Observability: RDS Proxy and X-Ray

concepts.heading: The Connection Storm Problem
concepts.body: Serverless and highly elastic compute like Lambda can scale out to thousands of concurrent executions almost instantly, and if each execution opens its own direct database connection, a traditional relational database can quickly exhaust its maximum connection limit, causing too many connections errors even though the database itself isn't overloaded on CPU or memory. This connection-exhaustion problem is specific to the mismatch between elastic, bursty compute and a database's fixed connection ceiling, and recognizing that mismatch in a scenario is the trigger for reaching for RDS Proxy.

concepts.heading: RDS Proxy as a Managed Connection Pool
concepts.body: Amazon RDS Proxy sits between the application and the database, maintaining a warm, efficiently managed pool of actual database connections and multiplexing many client connections from Lambda or EC2 onto that smaller pool, which prevents connection exhaustion during traffic spikes. It requires no code changes beyond pointing the connection string at the proxy endpoint instead of the database directly, and it also improves failover behavior by preserving application connections and automatically routing them to the new primary, so the application doesn't need custom reconnection logic.

concepts.heading: AWS X-Ray for Distributed Tracing
concepts.body: AWS X-Ray traces individual requests as they travel across a distributed application's components, whether Lambda functions, ECS tasks, or EC2-hosted services, recording the timing and outcome of each hop and assembling that data into a Service Map that visualizes dependencies and highlights where latency or errors are concentrated. This is invaluable for microservices architectures where a single slow user request might touch a dozen internal services, and pinpointing which one is actually responsible for added latency would be extremely difficult from logs alone.

concepts.heading: Observability as a Design Requirement
concepts.body: Both RDS Proxy and X-Ray reflect a broader theme in Domain 2: resilience isn't only about failing over cleanly, it's also about being able to see, diagnose, and manage a distributed system's behavior under load. X-Ray answers where a problem is coming from after the fact, while RDS Proxy prevents an entire class of connection-related failures before they happen; together they represent the reactive and proactive sides of running elastic, distributed applications reliably in production.

examPoints: A scenario describing too many connections errors from a database caused by a burst of Lambda invocations points specifically to RDS Proxy for connection pooling, not simply resizing the database instance.
A scenario describing the need to pinpoint which microservice is causing latency in a multi-service request chain points to AWS X-Ray's distributed tracing and Service Map.

quiz.q: During a traffic spike, thousands of concurrent Lambda invocations attempt to connect directly to an RDS database, causing 'too many connections' errors. What is the recommended fix?
choices: Simply increase the size of the RDS instance
Introduce Amazon RDS Proxy to pool and manage connections
Remove all concurrency limits on the Lambda function
quiz.explain: RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections, which directly addresses connection exhaustion from bursty, highly concurrent compute. Increasing instance size doesn't raise the connection ceiling the way pooling does, and removing concurrency limits would make the problem worse.

quiz.q: A microservices-based application experiences intermittent latency, and the team needs to identify exactly which service in the request chain is responsible. What tool should they use?
choices: AWS X-Ray to trace requests end-to-end
quiz.explain: X-Ray traces individual requests across every service they touch and visualizes the results in a Service Map, making it purpose-built for pinpointing the source of latency. CloudWatch Logs alone would require manually correlating logs across many services without that structured tracing.

days.recap: RDS Proxy pools database connections to prevent exhaustion from bursty compute like Lambda and preserves connections through failover, while X-Ray traces requests end-to-end across distributed services to pinpoint the source of latency or errors.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Resilient Architectures

concepts.heading: Decoupling Recap: SQS, API Gateway, and Compute Choices
concepts.body: Domain 2 began with loose coupling: SQS buffers bursty traffic between producers and consumers, API Gateway fronts APIs with built-in throttling and caching, and the compute layer itself can be decoupled using Lambda for short event-driven tasks, ECS/EKS for containerized workloads, and Fargate to remove server management from either orchestrator. The throughline is that isolating components behind asynchronous boundaries or managed abstractions prevents a failure or spike in one place from cascading into everything connected to it.

concepts.heading: Orchestration and Traffic Distribution Recap
concepts.body: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with built-in retries and full execution visibility, while Application Load Balancer distributes and routes Layer 7 traffic based on path or host, continuously removing unhealthy targets via health checks. Together they represent two different resilience mechanisms: one coordinates a sequence of operations reliably, and the other keeps traffic flowing only to healthy compute at any given moment.

concepts.heading: High Availability Recap: AZs, Multi-AZ, and Route 53
concepts.body: The core high-availability pattern is spreading resources across at least two Availability Zones, RDS Multi-AZ provides automatic database failover for availability specifically, not read scaling, which is the Read Replica's job, and Route 53's Failover and Weighted routing policies extend resilience patterns to the DNS layer, enabling automated disaster recovery cutover and gradual canary rollouts respectively.

concepts.heading: Connection Resilience and Visibility Recap
concepts.body: RDS Proxy solves the specific problem of elastic compute exhausting a database's connection limit, while X-Ray provides the distributed tracing needed to diagnose where latency or errors originate in a microservices architecture. Both reflect that resilience in Domain 2 covers not just whether something fails over but also whether it can handle bursty load gracefully and whether operators can see what's actually happening when something goes wrong.

examPoints: For any Domain 2 scenario, first identify what kind of problem is being described: a sudden traffic spike, a component failure, or an AZ/region outage, since each maps to a distinct family of services.
Domain 2 is worth 26% of the exam; the RDS Multi-AZ versus Read Replica distinction and the SQS standard versus FIFO distinction are two of the most frequently retested pairs across this domain.

quiz.q: Which service buffers a sudden burst of incoming requests so a backend can process them at a sustainable rate?
quiz.explain: SQS decouples producers from consumers asynchronously, absorbing bursts so the backend isn't overwhelmed. The other services address DNS routing, tracing, and certificates, none of which buffer request bursts.

quiz.q: Which configuration allows a relational database to fail over automatically to another Availability Zone with minimal downtime?
choices: A single-AZ standby server kept manually
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ deployments maintain a synchronously replicated standby and handle failover automatically. A Read Replica exists to scale reads, not to serve as the automatic failover target.

days.recap: Domain 2 wraps up around decoupling (SQS/compute choices), orchestration and traffic routing (Step Functions/ALB), high availability (Multi-AZ/Route 53), and connection resilience plus observability (RDS Proxy/X-Ray).

days.title: High-Performance Storage: S3, EFS, and EBS

concepts.heading: Amazon S3: Object Storage at Scale
concepts.body: Amazon S3 stores data as objects within buckets, scales to effectively unlimited capacity without any provisioning, and offers multiple storage classes ranging from Standard for frequently accessed data down to Glacier tiers for long-term archives, letting cost track access frequency. S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront's global edge network to speed up uploads over long distances by routing them through the nearest edge location onto AWS's backbone network. Because many applications, and often many separate compute instances, can read and write to the same bucket concurrently, S3 is the default choice for shared, durable storage of large volumes of unstructured data.

concepts.heading: Amazon EFS: Shared File Storage
concepts.body: Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system that can be mounted concurrently by many EC2 instances, containers, or even Lambda functions, all reading and writing to the same shared directory structure at once. Its capacity grows and shrinks automatically as data is added or removed, with no pre-provisioning of storage size required, and it supports multiple performance and throughput modes to match different workload shapes. EFS is the answer whenever a scenario specifically requires multiple compute instances to share a single, POSIX-compliant file system concurrently, something EBS cannot do.

concepts.heading: Amazon EBS: Block Storage for a Single Instance
concepts.body: Amazon EBS provides block-level storage volumes that attach to a single EC2 instance, with the narrow exception of Multi-Attach io2 volumes designed for cluster-aware filesystems, functioning like a virtual hard disk with persistent storage independent of the instance's lifecycle. EBS offers multiple volume types tuned for different workloads: gp3 for general-purpose balanced performance, io2 for high, consistent IOPS demanded by databases, and st1/sc1 for throughput-oriented, infrequently accessed workloads like big data or log processing at a lower cost per gigabyte.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between S3, EFS, and EBS
concepts.body: The clean mental separation is: S3 for object storage accessed by many applications or clients over HTTP-style APIs, EFS for a POSIX file system shared concurrently by multiple compute instances, and EBS for a single instance's dedicated block storage, such as a boot volume or database data volume needing consistent low-latency IOPS. A scenario mentioning that multiple EC2 instances need to read and write the same directory is an EFS scenario, while one mentioning a database engine's underlying storage on a single instance is an EBS scenario, and mixing these two up is a common wrong-answer trap.

examPoints: A requirement for multiple EC2 instances to concurrently share and write to the same file directory is EFS's defining use case, which EBS cannot support outside its narrow Multi-Attach exception.
A requirement for a single instance's boot volume or a high-IOPS database volume points to EBS, with io2 specifically called out when very high, consistent IOPS is emphasized.

quiz.q: Multiple EC2 instances need to concurrently read and write to the exact same file system directory. Which storage service should be used?
quiz.explain: EFS is a managed NFS file system designed to be mounted and shared concurrently by multiple instances. EBS volumes attach to a single instance in nearly all cases, so they cannot serve this shared-access requirement.

quiz.q: A single EC2 instance runs a high-performance transactional database that requires consistently high IOPS. Which storage option is most appropriate?
quiz.explain: EBS io2 volumes are purpose-built for high, consistent IOPS workloads like transactional databases on a single instance. EFS and S3 are not designed for the low-latency block-level access a database engine requires.

days.recap: S3 is scalable object storage for large volumes of shared data across many storage classes, EFS is a managed file system shared concurrently across multiple instances, and EBS is block storage dedicated to a single instance with performance characteristics that vary by volume type.

days.title: Elastic and High-Performance Compute: Batch, EMR, and Auto Scaling

concepts.heading: AWS Batch for Managed Job Scheduling
concepts.body: AWS Batch manages the entire lifecycle of running large numbers of batch computing jobs: it queues submitted jobs, automatically provisions the optimal type and quantity of compute resources, choosing among EC2, Spot Instances, or Fargate, needed to run them, and scales that compute down again when the queue empties, all without requiring the team to manage a cluster manually. It's particularly well suited to workloads composed of many independent jobs, such as rendering, simulations, or genomics processing, where the exact compute needs vary job to job and provisioning it manually would be wasteful or slow.

concepts.heading: Amazon EMR for Big Data Frameworks
concepts.body: Amazon EMR runs big data processing frameworks like Apache Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Presto on managed clusters, handling cluster provisioning, framework installation, and scaling so data engineering teams can focus on the processing logic instead of infrastructure. EMR clusters can mix On-Demand and Spot Instances within the same cluster to reduce cost for fault-tolerant, distributed processing jobs, and can be spun up transiently for a single job and terminated afterward or run as a long-lived cluster depending on the workload pattern.

concepts.heading: EC2 Auto Scaling Fundamentals
concepts.body: EC2 Auto Scaling maintains a fleet of instances within configured minimum, desired, and maximum capacity bounds, automatically launching or terminating instances in response to metrics like average CPU utilization, request count, or a custom CloudWatch metric via target tracking, step, or scheduled scaling policies. This is the foundational mechanism for elastically matching compute capacity to real-time demand, and it also works hand in hand with health checks, from EC2 or an attached load balancer, to replace instances that fail, keeping the fleet at its desired healthy capacity automatically.

concepts.heading: AWS Auto Scaling as a Unified Scaling Service
concepts.body: While EC2 Auto Scaling manages EC2 fleets specifically, the broader AWS Auto Scaling service can create and manage scaling policies across multiple resource types at once, including DynamoDB tables, ECS services, and Aurora replicas, from a single unified scaling plan. This distinction matters when a scenario describes coordinating scaling across several different service types together rather than just an EC2 fleet in isolation, since it points to AWS Auto Scaling's cross-service scope rather than the EC2-specific feature alone.

examPoints: A scenario describing thousands of independent batch jobs that need to run without manually managing the underlying cluster or compute type points to AWS Batch.
A scenario describing Hadoop or Spark-based big data processing on a managed cluster points to Amazon EMR specifically, distinct from AWS Batch's generic job-queue model.

quiz.q: A company needs to run thousands of independent batch processing jobs and wants AWS to automatically provision the optimal compute resources for each without managing a cluster manually. What service fits best?
choices: A permanently running Amazon EMR cluster
Sequential execution on a single EC2 instance
AWS Lambda for every job regardless of duration
quiz.explain: AWS Batch manages job queuing and automatically provisions the right compute resources for each job. A permanently running EMR cluster is built for big data frameworks, not generic batch job scheduling, and Lambda has execution-duration limits unsuited to long batch jobs.

quiz.q: A data engineering team needs to run large-scale Apache Spark and Hadoop processing jobs on a managed cluster. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: EMR is purpose-built for managed big data frameworks like Spark and Hadoop. AWS Batch is a generic job scheduler and doesn't provide the Spark/Hadoop cluster environment directly.

days.recap: AWS Batch automatically provisions compute for queued independent jobs, EMR runs Spark/Hadoop workloads on managed clusters, and EC2 Auto Scaling, extended by AWS Auto Scaling across multiple services, automatically adjusts capacity to match demand based on metrics.

days.title: High-Performance Databases: Aurora, DynamoDB, and ElastiCache

concepts.heading: Amazon Aurora's Performance Advantages
concepts.body: Amazon Aurora is a MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible managed relational database whose storage layer automatically grows in increments up to 128 TB and is replicated six ways across three Availability Zones for durability, delivering higher throughput than standard RDS on comparable hardware. Aurora supports up to 15 low-latency read replicas, compared to five on standard RDS, that share the same underlying storage volume as the writer, which means replica lag is typically much lower since replicas don't need to independently replay every write.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Performance and DAX
concepts.body: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database delivering consistent single-digit-millisecond latency at virtually any scale, provided the table's partition key is designed to spread requests evenly and avoid hot partitions that would throttle throughput. For workloads needing even faster reads, DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory caching layer purpose-built for DynamoDB that reduces read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for cacheable, repeated read patterns, without requiring any application logic changes beyond pointing at the DAX endpoint.

concepts.heading: ElastiCache for Database Offloading
concepts.body: Amazon ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching using Redis or Memcached, typically deployed in front of a relational or NoSQL database to absorb repeated reads of the same hot data, dramatically reducing both database load and end-user response time. Redis additionally supports data structures, persistence, and replication features that make it suitable as a lightweight primary data store or session store in its own right, while Memcached offers a simpler, purely multi-threaded caching model without those extra features.

concepts.heading: Read Replicas vs Caching: Two Ways to Scale Reads
concepts.body: Both Read Replicas, for RDS/Aurora, and ElastiCache reduce the load a primary database experiences from read traffic, but they work differently: a Read Replica is still a full database serving live queries, useful for reporting or analytics workloads that need SQL access to current data, while a cache stores the result of specific, frequently repeated queries in memory, intercepting requests before they ever reach the database engine at all. A scenario emphasizing that the exact same data is queried repeatedly is a strong hint toward caching, whereas a scenario about isolating reporting queries from production traffic points to a Read Replica instead.

examPoints: A scenario describing heavy read load on a database from repeatedly-requested identical data, causing degraded response times, points to introducing ElastiCache as a caching layer rather than simply scaling the database further.
A scenario requiring microsecond-level read latency specifically from DynamoDB points to enabling DAX rather than a generic caching solution.
